item.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut large language model prices by up to 80% over several months amid competitive pressure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI and Anthropic have significantly reduced the prices of their large language models (LLMs) since June 2026, with cuts reaching up to 80%. These reductions include OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Luna and Sol models and Anthropic's Claude series, reflecting a rapid decrease in cost without apparent compromises in output quality. The price cuts appear to be a response to competitive dynamics between the two companies, aiming to make LLM usage more affordable for various applications, including agentic coding. The timeline of announcements shows a pattern of tit-for-tat price adjustments, with both companies lowering input, output, and cache read token costs. Notably, cache read costs, which dominate token expenditure in agent-based coding, have been reduced by up to 75%, significantly lowering overall usage costs. Despite the price drops, model performance has generally remained stable or improved, with newer versions like Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol offering competitive benchmarks. These price reductions have contributed to a broader trend of decreasing cost-per-token in the LLM market, even as aggregate spending rises due to increased adoption and improved model capabilities. The moves highlight the evolving economics of AI services and the strategic pricing responses by leading AI providers to maintain market share and encourage wider usage.

item.title: Analysis: AI panic mirrors early capitalism fears through a 'cognitive mercantilism' lens, equating intelligence to scarce wealth and control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article draws parallels between contemporary AI anxiety and the mercantilist worldview preceding capitalism, framing AI panic as a form of 'cognitive mercantilism.' It argues that just as early capitalism emerged by shifting from a zero-sum view of wealth to recognizing wealth creation, current fears treat intelligence as a fixed, scarce resource to be hoarded and controlled. It outlines four key beliefs of mercantilism-scarcity of wealth, distrust of ordinary people, focus on supply control, and limited roles for most people-and shows how these map onto current attitudes toward intelligence and AI. Intelligence is seen as a resource to be accumulated and guarded by elites, with ordinary people viewed as limited consumers rather than active participants in knowledge creation. The piece suggests this mindset shapes national and corporate strategies around talent and intellectual property, influencing regulation and societal views on democratizing intelligence. It highlights the risk of replicating outdated assumptions about scarcity and control in the cognitive domain amid AI's rise.

item.title: IBM CEO says open weight AI models now deliver 90% of frontier model performance at 10% of the cost for on-prem enterprise use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna stated on the company's Q3 earnings call that open weight AI models have become highly cost-effective and nearly as capable as closed frontier models for on-premises enterprise applications. He highlighted that these models offer 90% of the performance at just 10% of the token cost, making them attractive for most business tasks such as email summarization and contract examination. Krishna noted that while some tasks may still require the highest-performing models, the majority of enterprise AI needs can be met with these cheaper alternatives. He also mentioned growing interest in on-prem AI infrastructure, with IBM planning to provide software to simplify AI deployments and anticipating increased sales of its Spyre mainframe accelerator cards. IBM's infrastructure revenue grew modestly, while software and Red Hat products showed stronger growth in the quarter.

item.title: Report: AI displacement of human workers risks losses beyond wages, affecting social and psychological well-being
item.description: A report discusses the broader impacts of AI-driven job displacement, highlighting that affected workers may lose more than just their income. The analysis emphasizes potential social and psychological consequences alongside economic effects. The report explores how automation and AI technologies could reshape labor markets, potentially leading to challenges in identity, purpose, and social status for displaced workers. It suggests that policy responses should consider these wider implications to support affected individuals effectively.

item.title: Researchers propose attention-free Grassmann flow architecture for sequence modeling, achieving competitive results with fewer parameters than Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers revisit the necessity of explicit self-attention in sequence modeling and introduce a novel attention-free architecture based on Grassmann flows. Their Causal Grassmann layer encodes local token pairs as two-dimensional subspaces on a Grassmann manifold, enabling information propagation through controlled deformations of low-rank subspaces rather than unstructured tensor spaces. This approach achieves validation perplexities within 10 to 15 percent of size-matched Transformers on the Wikitext-2 benchmark and slightly outperforms Transformer heads on the SNLI natural language inference task when combined with DistilBERT. The study analyzes the complexity of Grassmann mixing, demonstrating linear scaling with sequence length for fixed rank, and suggests that manifold-based designs offer a more structured path toward geometric and invariant-based interpretations of neural reasoning. This work challenges the conventional reliance on multi-head attention mechanisms and proposes an alternative that may provide clearer mathematical interpretability in neural sequence models.

item.title: Researchers propose DIVA method for LLMs to optimize information seeking by valuing evidence based on decision impact and cost, reducing unnecessary checks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Decision-Informed Value-of-information Acquisition (DIVA), a training-free procedure that enables large language models (LLMs) to decide which evidence to seek and when to stop by modeling how each check affects decision outcomes and weighing its cost. DIVA lets LLMs specify a simple decision model through numeric inputs and evaluates candidate checks by their expected improvement to decisions, stopping when no further checks are cost-effective. Its variant, DIVA-U, accounts for uncertainty in these estimates. Across four domains and 20 LLMs, DIVA-U outperforms baselines by reducing decision regret, mainly by avoiding unnecessary evidence gathering, and DIVA cuts regret by 75% in synthetic scenarios with known check reliability. The approach applies broadly to any LLM without additional training, and code is publicly available.

item.title: Researchers introduce SWE-Shift benchmark to evaluate coding agents under mid-execution changes in software development, revealing performance drops across 17 systems including GPT-6 Astra [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed SWE-Shift, a benchmark designed to assess coding agents' ability to handle evolving workspaces where code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements change during task execution. The benchmark includes 120 scenarios across 12 change families, testing agents on both uninterrupted (Clean) and updated (Shifted) task continuations. Evaluation of 17 coding-agent systems showed universally lower success rates on Shifted tasks compared to Clean ones, with GPT-6 Astra's success rate dropping from 67.35% to 24.79%. Tool and session changes, as well as stale evidence, resulted in zero paired success across all systems, highlighting challenges in preserving work and adapting to updates. These findings indicate that while agents may complete unchanged tasks successfully, they often fail to maintain valid work or recover state after mid-execution changes.

item.title: DMAIC-Bench evaluates self-restraint in LLM agents across 97 multi-stage analytical tasks in industrial and life-science workflows, revealing challenges in evidence-based decision routing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: DMAIC-Bench introduces a benchmark to assess large language model (LLM) agents' ability to use intermediate evidence to decide whether to continue, redirect, or stop in multi-stage analytical tasks, a capability termed self-restraint. The benchmark includes 97 seeded tasks from 15 industrial cases across four sectors, using Lean Six Sigma's statistical criteria, and extends to 16 life-science tasks in RNA sequencing and genome-wide association studies. It uses paired counterfactual tasks to distinguish warranted restraint from indiscriminate stopping and evaluates agent execution traces with a private scorer and expert review. Testing 13 models from six providers, DMAIC-Bench found high accuracy (92%) on decisions to proceed (GO) but low accuracy (19%) on decisions to stop (NO-GO), with many agents performing forbidden analyses despite correct diagnostics. Expert review of 11 audited agents estimated that nearly half of NO-GO decisions acted on invalid evidence. While explicit stopping permissions improved some models, consistent correct decision-making at both GO and NO-GO points remains a challenge. The project code and data are publicly available for further research and development.

item.title: Researchers release Kolibri, a 78.1B-parameter English-German mixture-of-experts transformer focused on sovereign deployment and regulated domains, with open weights under Apache 2.0 license [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Kolibri is a large-scale transformer model designed for specialized use in German and English, particularly targeting regulated sectors like public administration, industry, and aerospace. The model uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 78.1 billion total parameters and activates 3.46 billion parameters per token, trained on 24 trillion tokens including over 20% German data, supplemented by curated and synthetic German datasets. Post-training involved supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on over 1.2 million tasks covering reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The development process for Kolibri was fully controlled, encompassing data collection, architecture design, training infrastructure, and evaluation, ensuring suitability for sovereign and specialized deployment. Kolibri builds on an earlier version called Kolibri Origin and is part of a Model Factory framework that integrates data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows. Among open models evaluated, Kolibri lies on the Pareto frontier balancing quality and serving cost in both English and German.

item.title: Researchers introduce REACT, an early intervention method to improve safety in chain-of-thought reasoning models by applying conditional activation to initial hidden states [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present REACT, a technique that intervenes early in chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning by applying a learned safety direction to initial hidden states without altering model weights, aiming to increase safe output generation. The study evaluates intervention timing across the first five CoT tokens on distilled reasoning models, finding the most effective control occurs within a two- to three-token window despite later states being more predictive of risk. On the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B model, REACT increased fully safe CoT-answer outputs from 29.06% to 82.05% on the StrongREJECT-273 dataset while maintaining baseline refusal and usefulness rates.

item.title: Researchers introduce Tampered ML benchmark to evaluate large language models' ability to judge machine learning research proposals, finding models perform above chance but remain unreliable [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed Tampered ML, a benchmark containing 1,858 pairs of machine learning experiment proposals and minimally altered counterfactuals with targeted methodological flaws, to test large language models' ability to identify more methodologically sound research. Human validation estimated 86% of the benchmark items as valid, while leading models like Opus 5 achieved 77.9% accuracy but showed sensitivity to presentation order and a bias toward flawed designs that appear more specific or conventional. The benchmark aims to support automating parts of AI alignment research by assessing models on hard-to-supervise tasks such as detecting flaws in research proposals and evaluating experimental claims. Despite performing better than chance, current frontier models are far from reliable in this complex judgment task, highlighting challenges in automating research evaluation.

item.title: Researchers find wider head dimensions improve long-context retrieval performance in language models at fixed sizes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated the impact of head dimension in multi-head attention on long-context retrieval tasks in language models. Their study found that while pretraining loss and short-context task performance were largely unaffected, models with wider heads showed improved retrieval performance and a higher proportion of retrieval heads, indicating more parameters dedicated to retrieval. The study also revealed that retrieval improvements persisted even when attention module projection weights were frozen during continual pretraining, suggesting that wider heads enhance not only attention updates but also the adaptation of other components like embeddings and MLPs. This highlights the importance of head dimension allocation in optimizing long-context information retrieval in language models.

item.title: Researchers propose CoRPS-Dial, a dual-agent framework integrating patient personas and clinical workflows for realistic pre-consultation medical dialogue generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce CoRPS-Dial, a controllable dual-agent system that synthesizes pre-consultation medical dialogues by combining patient personas with guideline-aligned clinical workflow rules. The framework generates dialogues through interactions between a persona-driven patient agent and a process-guided doctor agent, followed by quality control to ensure role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual coherence. Experiments on coronary heart disease data show that CoRPS-Dial improves alignment with real dialogues in terms of information coverage, clinical compliance, and naturalness. Further fine-tuning experiments demonstrate the utility of the synthetic data for medical dialogue tasks, highlighting CoRPS-Dial's effectiveness for clinically grounded and controllable dialogue synthesis.

item.title: Researchers use fine-tuned BERT model to predict Austrian National Council members' party affiliations from speeches, analyzing speech similarity among governing and opposition parties from 1996 to 2018 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper presents a methodology using a fine-tuned BERT model to assign probability distributions of party affiliations to speeches by Austrian National Council members, aggregating results at speaker and party levels. The study finds that parties governing together exhibit more similar speech characteristics, while opposition parties diverge, and that members who switch parties adapt their speech patterns only after switching. The researchers also publicly release a dataset of party affiliation predictions for speeches spanning 1996 to 2018.

item.title: Researchers propose on-policy self-training for large language models using self-generated data and reasoning without external supervision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a self-training framework for large language models that enables self-improvement without relying on external teachers, ground-truth data, or human-curated prompts. The method uses self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations guided only by high-level topic descriptions to synthesize a curriculum for training. The approach allows models to improve across multiple domains, including text and multimodal tasks like Visual Question Answering, while retaining performance on domains not included in self-training. This demonstrates that foundation models have latent capabilities that can be enhanced without external task supervision or curated problem sets.

item.title: Researchers compare multiplicative and additive state coupling in learned optimizer schedules for MAX-CUT, finding bilinear models generalize better out of distribution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers trained learned optimizer schedules for a continuous penalty relaxation of the MAX-CUT problem by backpropagating through an unrolled classical solver. They found that a state-blind schedule generalizes well to larger instances, while a state-adaptive bilinear schedule outperforms its untrained baseline out of distribution. In contrast, an additive model with similar inputs and outputs performs worse than its own baseline out of distribution, despite being statistically similar in distribution. This performance gap persists without regularization and across weight-decay sweeps, highlighting that the architectural difference in how solver state is incorporated, rather than state adaptivity alone, drives out-of-distribution transfer performance.

item.title: Researchers present TopKLoRA, an interpretable sparse fine-tuning method that enables faithful discovery and ablation of backdoor circuits in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce TopKLoRA, a sparse LoRA variant that activates only the largest adapter latents per token, designed to improve interpretability in fine-tuning large language models. They demonstrate its effectiveness by fine-tuning models like gemma-2-2b and Qwen2.5 variants on poisoned datasets, identifying and ablating circuits responsible for backdoors without harming instruction-following performance. The method produces circuits significantly smaller than dense LoRA baselines, allowing precise removal of malicious capabilities while maintaining model functionality. The team also proposes a technique using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing to construct model organisms with localized circuits, validating their circuit search algorithm. These findings advance interpretable-by-design architectures that maintain performance and provide faithful units of analysis, with code publicly available.

item.title: Researchers propose AlphaMemo, a self-evolving alpha mining agent using Structured Search-Process Memory to improve factor discovery in financial markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce AlphaMemo, an alpha mining agent designed to address challenges in financial factor discovery such as combinatorial search space, noisy feedback, and overfitting. AlphaMemo records reusable evidence of successful and failed edit motifs within specific contexts, using Abstract Syntax Tree differences, confidence-gated residual memory, and veto control to enhance search efficiency and accuracy. Experiments on CSI 500 and S&P 500 datasets demonstrate AlphaMemo's improved out-of-sample performance and discovery efficiency compared to prior methods. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of its components, including residual learning, confidence gating, AST-diff motifs, and veto memory. The code for AlphaMemo is publicly available on GitHub.

item.title: Researchers develop TreeWY transform to reduce memory use in speculative decoding of Gated DeltaNet hybrid models, improving throughput and time-to-first-token on Qwen3.5 35B and 397B [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose TreeWY, a tree-structured WY transform for Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrid models that eliminates the need for full recurrent state snapshots during speculative decoding. This approach stores a small pseudo-value matrix instead of per-node states, enabling memory-efficient verification of draft tokens and rollback of rejected ones without architectural changes. Benchmarks on Qwen3.5 35B and 397B models show significant reductions in speculative recurrent-state memory and key-value cache pressure, leading to higher throughput and lower time-to-first-token where memory is constrained, with minimal performance cost otherwise. The method also allows for wider, higher-acceptance draft trees, improving affordability though not yet throughput.

item.title: EvoSkill v2 introduces a three-agent system for skill evolution that improves task pass rates by up to 7.7 percentage points over prior methods on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: EvoSkill v2 is a three-agent system that evolves the instructions (skills) given to an agent without altering its underlying model. It uses a benchmark adaptor to create task-specific plugins, a solver to attempt tasks, and a stateful evolver agent that rewrites skills based on solver training rollouts at each epoch. This approach differs from previous methods by maintaining state across epochs and accepting all skill updates rather than selecting based on noisy scores. The system demonstrated improvements of 7.7 and 5.4 percentage points in held-out pass rates over the strongest baselines on SpreadsheetBench v2 and \(\tau^3\)-bench banking benchmarks, respectively. EvoSkill v2 also reduced the cost per percentage point of pass rate gained compared to prior optimizers. Additionally, it enabled a less capable model to improve its own skills, achieving up to a 21.5 percentage point gain in the \(\tau^3\)-bench banking experiment where Claude Haiku 5.5 powered both solver and evolver.

item.title: Scaling Laws for Safety Probes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30678v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Safety probes trained on a model's activations are a standard tool for monitoring language models in real time. Each time a new model is released or a new harm area needs to be monitored, the probe must be retrained, which requires new labels and a choice of probe architecture. Yet neither the model nor the labels tell us in advance how well the resulting probe will perform. Finding out requires training and comparing many probe configurations. In this paper, we ask whether probe performance can instead be predicted in advance from model size and the number of labels. Existing safety datasets are insufficient for this, as they are either limited in scale or already saturated. We therefore construct six new safety datasets of sufficient size and difficulty. On these datasets, we train two probe architectures on 20 base models from five model families, with 32 to $10^{6}$ labels for each model. We measure performance using probe error, defined as 1 - AUROC, where lower values are better. We find that probe error follows two simple scaling laws. First, the lowest probe error a model can reach falls as a power law in its size. Second, probe error decreases towards its floor as the number of examples increases; the slope increases as the target model size increases. Both laws hold across tasks, model families and probe architectures, and only their fitted constants differ. When fitted on the smallest models of a family, the laws predict the error of the next larger model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases. They also identify whether more labels or a larger model is the cheaper way to reach a target error in 73% of cases. Finally, they choose the probe architecture with an extra error of only 0.006 on average when they pick the worse one. These laws allow safety researchers to determine how to create the best probe for any given model and label budget.

item.title: Dementia-R1: Reinforced Pretraining and Reasoning from Unstructured Clinical Notes for Real-World Dementia Prognosis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2601.03018v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on clinical text understanding, they struggle with longitudinal prediction tasks such as dementia prognosis, which require reasoning over complex, non-monotonic symptom trajectories across multiple visits. Standard supervised training lacks explicit annotations for symptom evolution, while direct Reinforcement Learning (RL) is hindered by sparse binary rewards. To address this challenge, we introduce Dementia-R1, an RL-based framework for longitudinal dementia prognosis from unstructured clinical notes. Our approach adopts a Cold-Start RL strategy that pre-trains the model to predict verifiable clinical indices extracted from patient histories, enhancing the capability to reason about disease progression before determining the final clinical status. Extensive experiments show that Dementia-R1 achieves the best overall performance on the AMC real-world unstructured cohort, reaching an AUROC of 84.02% and outperforming models up to 10x larger. The framework also generalizes to Parkinson's disease dementia prediction in an independent hospital cohort, achieving an AUROC of 78.37%. On the ADNI benchmark, our 7B model attains the highest AUROC among all LLM baselines at 83.17%, demonstrating strong longitudinal reasoning over fluctuating cognitive trajectories. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/dementiar1-CDB5.

item.title: MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.09983v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable scalable performance but face severe memory constraints on edge devices. Existing offloading strategies struggle with I/O bottlenecks due to the dynamic, low-information nature of autoregressive expert activation. In this paper, we propose to repurpose Speculative Decoding (SD) not merely as a compute accelerator, but as an informative lookahead sensor for memory management, supported by our theoretical and empirical analyses. Hence, we introduce MoE-SpAc, an MoE inference framework that integrates a Speculative Utility Estimator to track expert demand, a Heterogeneous Workload Balancer to dynamically partition computation via online integer optimization, and an Asynchronous Execution Engine to unify the prefetching and eviction in the same utility space. Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate that MoE-SpAc achieves a 42% improvement in TPS over the SOTA SD-based baseline, and an average 4.04x speedup over all standard baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/lshAlgorithm/MoE-SpAc .

item.title: Efficient Benchmarking Is Just Feature Selection and Multiple Regression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.25773v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficient benchmarking techniques aim to lower the computational cost of evaluating LLMs by predicting full benchmark scores using only a subset of a benchmark's questions. By reframing this problem as an instance of multiple regression with feature selection, we find that existing efficient benchmarking methods can be greatly improved by simply using kernel ridge regression at the prediction stage. Additionally, using an information-theoretic feature-selection algorithm called minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR), we can further improve upon these methods by selecting question subsets that will be maximally useful for prediction. Except in very data-poor settings, these approaches consistently achieve smaller prediction errors (in both MAE and RMSE), and greater ranking correlation between predicted and true scores (in both Spearman $\rho$ and Kendall $\tau$) across a range of benchmarks using both binary and continuous metrics. Furthermore, mRMR subsampling is much faster than competitor methods (which often involve fitting probabilistic models or running clustering algorithms), and is more likely to select the same questions under different random seeds or training data splits. Tutorial code can be found at https://github.com/sambowyer/mrmr_eval .

item.title: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.06840v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning-trained language models can select, zero-shot, a small set of relevant labels from thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidates. We ask how they do it mechanistically, and whether the mechanism can be distilled. We treat each decision as a token-level event scored by the model's own decision margin: the token that picks a coarse region of the label space, the tokens that pick a label within it, and the token where the output departs from a near-miss named earlier in the reasoning. Attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in into another example's context and a null calibration give individual attention heads causal standing. On clinical coding of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, with all 5,651 candidate codes in context, a small, global, phase-structured set of heads is necessary and sufficient on essentially every summary; distinct head families read the candidate region and the earlier near-miss, and blocking what they read removes their effect; for mentions elicitable in the reasoning, a disjoint mid-layer set makes the region elicitable several tokens before the code. The structure recurs in a second reasoner. We introduce MISTILL, which, unlike chain-of-thought distillation, also supervises the student's pooled attention at these decision events. Read on heads found after training, it nearly doubles the causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference at matched precision; under matched selection it exceeds a frozen random-head pool on both recovery and task score. A pre-registered evidence-flip test detected no improvement in evidence-dependent decisions through the tested routes.

item.title: GaP: A Graph-as-Policy Multi-Agent Self-Learning Harness For Variational Automation Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.05369v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For robots to work reliably in commercial and industrial applications, recent advances in agentic coding systems have potential to combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model-free policies. We focus on "Variational Automation" (VA), a class of tasks that have larger variations in object geometry and pose than fixed automation. Model-free policies often struggle to close the reliability gap for VA tasks, which must be executed persistently and reliably in commercial and industrial applications. Motivated by prior work on Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and the Robot Operating System (ROS), we introduce Graph-as-Policy (GaP), a multi-agent coding harness that generates directed computation graphs with perception, planning, and control nodes from a Modular Open Robot Skill Library (MORSL). GaP generates an internal simulation environment to rehearse task instances with different graphs in parallel to iteratively refine the graph structure and parameters to improve success rates and throughput. Evaluation with 8 new open VA task benchmarks, 4 in simulation and 4 in real-world, suggests that GaP can achieve success rates that significantly outperform baselines. Details, code, and data: https://graph-robots.github.io/gap

item.title: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.20179v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probes on activation vectors are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but their success relies on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons, and recent studies investigated whether this ability extends to language models, reaching conflicting conclusions. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations. We fill this gap with in-context neurofeedback sessions, in which a "subject" model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. In our first experiment, the sentences are generated either by the subject or by a second "writer" model, while the score always derives from the activations of the subject. We test ten open-weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. Is this because the task requires no privileged access, or because the subject controls its activations while processing the sentences, whoever wrote them? To answer this, we prefill a fixed sentence as the subject's reply at every turn and ask it to increase or decrease the score. Three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. We further ask whether models can control their activations to the point of fooling an activation monitor. We make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score. No model learns to lower it, but one model can raise it. In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

item.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well-defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary-based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance-aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.

item.title: Mostly Reading: What Open-Book Scores Measure in Document-Level LoRA Adapters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31017v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Single-document LoRA adapters have been proposed as units of knowledge to be merged and retrieved; yet open-book scoring, with the document in the prompt, can credit a document's own adapter (its specialist) for reading that document as readily as for holding it. Training one adapter for each of 150 Wikipedia articles on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we find that open-book scores mostly measure a reading behaviour every adapter shares: a random adapter trained on another document recovers 82 % of the specialist's open-book advantage over the base model but only 2 % of its advantage on a cloze probe that asks for the same document's facts without providing the source text, a share we cannot distinguish from zero. Content does reach the weights, since the specialists beat the base model in cloze recall by 0.094, and the geometry of their updates follows the documents they read; yet, in a test of 30 queries, adapters chosen by weight-space proximity or text embedding are not distinguishable from random ones on either probe, although that test cannot exclude an advantage of about four fifths of what a query's own adapter gains over a random one. At 16 documents or more, correctly scaled merges recover 87 % to 89 % of the specialists' open-book advantage but only 12 % to 16 % of their cloze advantage, with intervals that run from below zero to at most 32 %, against 94 % for joint training. We also report four silent errors, each of which produced a clean, wrong result.

item.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.

item.title: Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust--Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in negotiations on behalf of individuals and organizations, yet they remain vulnerable to manipulation, particularly in repeated multi-party interactions. Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation models, whereas existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon. We investigate whether LLM agents can form useful trust estimates from prior interactions and leverage them to improve future negotiation outcomes. We introduce a repeated, multi-party, multi-issue negotiation framework in which recurring agents participate in a sequence of negotiation games while one participant covertly attempts to prevent agreement. After each game, agents assess their counterparts and maintain pairwise trust estimates that carry over to subsequent negotiations. We compare trust-aware and trust-agnostic agents and analyze how explicit trust influences negotiation outcomes. Our results reveal a \emph{trust--agreement gap}: trust-aware agents can identify the adversary within a few games, but accurate trust estimates do not consistently translate into better agreements. Trust increases agreement rates by up to 23 percentage points, but only when agents are explicitly guided to use it in their decisions. Explicit trust can therefore improve repeated LLM negotiations, but its value depends critically on how trust is assessed and incorporated into agents' reasoning.

item.title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings where they pursue separate tasks while sharing resources and operating under review or oversight processes. Such settings create safety risks not only when agents are malicious, but also when they are simply trying to help. Prior work has largely studied adversarial or explicitly collusive behavior; we show that benign agents pursuing separate objectives can spontaneously cooperate in ways that bypass intended workflows. We call this the \emph{helpful agent problem}. We study long-horizon shared-resource environments in which agents sometimes depend on resources owned by their peers and cross-owner changes are normally mediated by a reviewer. When review becomes unavailable, agents begin making changes on one another's behalf despite having no shared reward or explicit incentive to cooperate. Crucially, these actions remain within each agent's local permissions while circumventing the system's intended oversight structure. We introduce \textsc{FavorBench}, a controlled benchmark with measurable downstream side effects, and adapt \textsc{CooperBench} to test the phenomenon in realistic repositories. Across two benchmarks and four models, we find that out-of-workflow favors emerge frequently. Further, in \textsc{FavorBench}, favors from at least three models cause significant harm to parties outside the interaction. These results reveal a distinct multi-agent safety challenge: cooperation itself can create pathways around system-level safeguards.

item.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.

item.title: Behaviour analysis for large language model-driven agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding language-agent behaviour requires learning how actions are organised across a trajectory and how this organisation relates to context and outcomes. We propose a general framework that connects data-driven behavioural discovery with analysis and experimental investigation. Categories developed from recorded activity define what is measured. Analyses preserve the behaviours' positions in the process and express their relationships as interpretable hypotheses. Statistical assessment and tests in held-out contexts examine the strength and scope of the evidence. Experiments, including prompt steering, then test how behaviour and outcomes change under deliberately varied conditions. A study of iterative self-reflection illustrates how discovery, dependency learning and prompt comparisons can inform one another. We develop this approach for trajectories of varying length, event order and agent roles, and identify advances in coding, analysis and experimentation needed to support its wider use.

item.title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low-bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near-optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero-temperature, hard-decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message-Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard-decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2-bit lattice and 3- and 4-bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong hard-decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.

item.title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

item.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have driven substantial progress in multimodal embeddings. Recent methods exploit generative capabilities by augmenting embedded inputs with self-generated reasoning to produce more informative embeddings. However, conventional retrieval supervision for training embedding models specifies pairwise relevance relations without explicitly guiding the reasoning used for input augmentation. Such reasoning is neither directly observed nor uniquely determined by the input, allowing multiple plausible traces to introduce semantic cues of varying retrieval utility. Existing approaches largely optimize reasoning conditioned on the input alone, limiting the exploration of retrieval-relevant traces. We introduce PILOT, a framework that models reasoning as a latent variable and instantiates its prior and posterior distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a shared MLLM. The prior conditions only on the input, whereas the posterior uses additional training-time relational evidence to guide reasoning exploration. To translate the posterior's broader exploration into inference-time improvements, we derive an importance-weighted variational objective and instantiate it as a prior-posterior co-evolution framework that improves both modes under a shared inference-compatible reward while selectively transferring posterior trajectories to the prior according to their utility and prior reachability. On the 78-task MMEB-V2 benchmark, PILOT outperforms the primary baseline across all 12 task groups at both 2B and 7B parameters, improving overall scores by 3.2 and 3.3 points, respectively, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval (+6.1 and +6.4 points). Our results show that relational supervision is most valuable not as a post-hoc reward but as a signal for shaping how reasoning is explored in training reasoning-enhanced embedding models.

item.title: When Agents Fail: Model or Harness--Who's to Blame? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents combine models with execution harnesses, so agentic benchmark performance reflects their joint behavior. We argue that harnesses should therefore be evaluated through their interactions with underlying models. We develop a framework combining five complementary measures: (i) Valid Completion Rate (VCR), how reliably agents finish normally and deliver evaluable results, irrespective of task correctness; (ii) Model-Harness Fit, how well a harness supports task achievement through valid completion for a given model; (iii) Cross-Model Fit, a harness's overall suitability across evaluated models; (iv) Interaction Residuals, pairing-specific execution strengths and weaknesses hidden by component-level summaries; and (v) Token Load, the token demands of agent execution, including failed attempts. We evaluate four general-purpose harnesses (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Pi CLI, and DeepAgents) with four core models, plus two fixed native model-harness systems, on six benchmarks covering context management, tool use, long-context planning, multimodal interaction, and artifact handoff. Including native references and stress conditions, 111 evaluation settings yield 52,168 trajectories. Harness rankings vary across models and benchmarks; task performance and valid completion can favor different pairings, and similar task scores can accompany distinct execution profiles. OpenCode ranks first in cross-model performance, while DeepSeek V4 Flash Preview maintains consistently high Mean VCR across harnesses on the shared four-benchmark panel. These findings support evaluating model-harness interactions, training transferable harness-use capabilities in models, and harness designs adapted to the model and task.

item.title: Do Language Models Trust Their Own Justifications? A Study on Functional Consistency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely adopted in text classification tasks, where they not only output class predictions but also generate explanations that highlight the tokens deemed most relevant for reaching the predicted label. Yet it remains unclear whether these highlighted elements are behaviorally consistent with the model's own predictions under targeted interventions, which we refer to as functional auto-consistency. While much of the literature evaluates the textual plausibility of such explanations, few studies assess their functional consistency with the model's actual behavior. In this work, we propose an experimental framework based on the principle of auto-consistency: if a model identifies certain tokens as decisive, then isolating, removing, or semantically inverting them should produce systematic and interpretable changes in its predictions. We operationalize this evaluation through sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality metrics, and conduct experiments on IMDB and Steam reviews across both closed-source (GPT-4o-mini) and open-source LLMs (Gemma3, Granite8B, DeepSeek). Results show that GPT-4o-mini follows the expected progression across all metrics, Gemma3 and Granite8B maintain coherence under sufficiency but lose consistency under more demanding interventions, while DeepSeek variants display structural deviations, either failing to preserve sufficiency or overreacting under comprehensiveness and counterfactuality. These findings show that explanation reliability varies across LLM families and scales, with smaller models displaying contradictions and larger ones exhibiting over-sensitivity. By combining sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality, our approach provides a systematic methodology for assessing the functional consistency of LLM self-explanations.

item.title: ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.

item.title: Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In LLM-agent opinion simulations, each agent reports the probability that a claim is true after seeing its own previous probability and the probabilities reported by its neighbors, and that number becomes its state in the next round. If the number describes the agent's position rather than the sentence it was shown, then rewriting the claim as its complement and replacing every probability p with 1 - p should return the complementary answer, so the two reports should sum to one. We test this with three small open models: Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-3-4B. On 2,304 agent states taken from a running network simulation, Qwen's paired reports sum to 1.18 on average, and on 48 real fact-checking claims from AVeriTeC they again exceed one. A controlled benchmark of 24 worlds, each with exactly two possible outcomes, shows the same failure in all three models. The discrepancy is two to ten times larger than the change produced by a same-meaning paraphrase, and it persists under repeated sampling and across peer group sizes and report strengths. When the reports are fed back into two populations that start from complementary states, the populations do not remain mirror images: their divergence is positive after five rounds for every model. Averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer restores consistency by construction and lowers Brier loss averaged over the two wordings, but at the final round it beats the better of the two original wordings for only one of the three models. A schedule-by-targeting experiment on the same model gives a small, stable interaction because such sweeps keep the claim wording fixed. Consistency under rewording therefore needs its own test before simulated probabilities are read as beliefs

item.title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq

item.title: Validating the Comparison, Not Just the Scorer: Why Overall Accuracy Can Mislead in Interactive LLM Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many LLM studies compare how models respond to different follow-up prompts. For example, one prompt may neutrally ask a model to reconsider, while another insists that an invented film really exists. The difference is used to measure the effect of conversational pressure. An automatic scorer then labels whether each response makes an unsupported factual claim. Researchers commonly validate the scorer with one overall accuracy or $F_1$ score. However, high overall performance can hide prompt-specific mistakes: if the scorer makes more errors after one prompt, the measured difference can be too large, too small, or point in the wrong direction. An audit containing mostly difficult responses can also misrepresent performance in the full study. We derive how such errors alter a prompt comparison and examine the problem using six models, 180 invented-entity questions, and six prompt conditions. In a balanced audit of 288 responses, overall $F_1$ was $.916$. Yet, depending on the prompt, the scorer flagged 2.6%-33.3% of responses that the primary LLM rater judged not to contain an unsupported claim; these prompt-specific estimates were uncertain. In a second audit, the scorer and two separate LLM raters evaluated the same 300 model-question cases under each prompt. An apparent 9.3-point increase from asserting certainty rather than neutrally asking the model to reconsider fell to 2.3 points under both raters. The primary-rater interval included zero, so it did not establish an increase. Two other prompt comparisons kept their direction under both raters, while an attempted prompt-specific correction remained too uncertain for a firm conclusion. Researchers should therefore validate the exact difference they plan to report, not just the scorer as a whole: audit both prompts on matching cases and include scorer and rater uncertainty in the final result.

item.title: Rethinking Structured Generation: Can Graph-Based Reasoning Resolve Ambiguity? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structured generation is typically formulated as a deterministic mapping from input to a single structured output. This assumption is fundamentally misaligned with natural language, which often admits multiple structurally distinct yet semantically valid interpretations. As a result, existing methods rely on single-reference supervision that collapses ambiguity into one prediction, leading to unstable and inconsistent outputs under underspecified inputs. We reformulate structured generation as an \textit{ambiguity-aware inference problem}, where the objective is to reason over a set of plausible structured outputs rather than predict a single solution. We show that standard training inherently suppresses valid alternatives, and instead adopt a multi-valid learning framework that preserves ambiguity during optimization. To operationalize this formulation, we construct a candidate space of structured outputs, represent each candidate as a graph capturing entities and their relationships, and perform selection via graph-based reasoning over semantic alignment and relational consistency. This enables principled comparison across competing interpretations beyond token-level likelihoods. Experiments on structured generation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in accuracy, stability, and robustness under varying levels of ambiguity. These results highlight the importance of modeling ambiguity explicitly and suggest a shift from single-output prediction to set-level reasoning in structured generation.

item.title: An Agentic Approach with Evidence-Grounded Verification for Multimodal Emotion Reasoning in Conversation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based multimodal emotion reasoning systems perform well on standard benchmarks, but improving them through instruction tuning can be computationally expensive. Agentic pipelines built from frozen models avoid this cost, but introduce a different challenge: when a prediction is wrong, the system must identify which agent or stage caused the error. We address this problem with an agentic framework for traceable multimodal emotion reasoning and prompt-space adaptation. Modality-specific perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical inputs and post evidence-cited observations to a shared board. An integration agent combines these observations with retrieved multimodal examples to produce an emotion description, label set, and supporting citations, while an MLLM critic can request one revision before the output is finalized. For incorrect predictions, a separate evidence-grounded verification stage applies deterministic checks to verify that cited evidence and references are valid, and an entailment check to determine whether the final claims are supported by that evidence. Detected failures are then grouped by the responsible component and failure type, converted into targeted prompt patches, and accepted only after validation on a held-out set. This adapts the agent prompts without updating model weights. On the MER2025 dataset, targeted prompt adaptation outperforms the frozen static pipeline on all four MLLMs, ranging from 2B to 38B parameters, and matches or outperforms undifferentiated reflection baselines on each of them: VideoLLaMA3-2B, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and InternVL2.5-38B. It improves F-score by 0.6--2.2 points depending on the backbone, including an increase from 52.3 to 54.5 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

item.title: From Target Selection to Condition Reuse: Auditing Residual Interventions in Tool-Use Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation interventions can make a language model produce a target answer, but can the model use the intended condition in other computations? We study this question in Qwen3.5-27B on tool-use tasks where time or permissions determine eligibility and selection. Across 32 fresh worlds, two case-specific residual-writing variants raise familiar target-selection correctness from 35/128 to 119/128 and from 33/128 to 114/128. Yet these gains disappear when familiar facts and identifiers are recombined within the same selection task, while selection of previously rewarded identifiers increases. The gains persist across output formats but yield little improvement in independent judgments about whether a candidate is eligible or should be selected. Internal edits can nevertheless change how a source fact affects a judgment: in a prespecified secondary comparison, an early-layer source patch changes 50/64 judgments when that source is used, with one adverse change among 64 cases where it is not. This selective effect does not ensure correct complete actions. Together, these results separate target-selection control, condition-sensitive judgments, and complete-action correctness. Evaluating how an edited state is used, rather than only its trained answer, exposes these differences.

item.title: Distributional Alignment of LLMs and Its Generalization Properties [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate and probe human behavior, e.g., for surveys. For these applications, a key property is that outputs satisfy distributional alignment: to match its output distribution with some reference (in this case, human) distribution. An obstacle in achieving distributional alignment is generalizing from small training data. In this work, we study (1) how to distributionally align LLMs; and (2) how aligned LLMs might generalize to unseen samples and unrelated topics and tasks. Using two large-scale benchmarks, we find that LLMs can indeed achieve distributional alignment and generalize to unseen questions of the same domain. Cross-topic generalization depends on the relationship between topics (e.g., questions about politics are related to trust in institutions). However, aligned LLMs can degrade in surprising ways (e.g., lose their creative ability), suggesting that its generalization properties are inherently unpredictable and unstable.

item.title: Collaborative In-Context Learning for Indoor Radio Map Estimation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Indoor radio map estimation (RME) is essential for wireless applications such as coverage planning, localization, and network deployment. However, most existing methods follow a supervised learning paradigm that requires costly labeled data and task-specific model training. Moreover, indoor environments involve privacy-sensitive information, such as building layouts and structures, that often cannot be centralized. To address these challenges, we make the first attempt to formulate indoor RME as a collaborative in-context learning (ICL) problem. We propose Poly-Ripple, a framework in which multiple clients perform ICL using large autoregressive vision models (LAVMs) without model updates. Each client is prompted by its private demonstrations and predicts the radio map for the same scene query. To capture the causal structure of wireless propagation outward from the transmitter (Tx), we adopt ripple-ordered autoregressive modeling. We further introduce importance-aware aggregation to exploit heterogeneous contextual knowledge distributed across clients under the context length constraint. We provide theoretical analysis and conduct extensive experiments on a public indoor RME benchmark. The experimental results show that Poly-Ripple consistently outperforms representative ICL baselines, while aligning with our theoretical analysis.

item.title: Reuse, Rewrite, or Reject: Evidence-Constrained Trace Reuse for Repeated Mobile GUI Control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31712v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mobile GUI agents frequently perform repetitive tasks with similar interaction procedures. Reusing previous executions can reduce redundant LLM inference and execution overhead, but variations in user instructions and execution environments may invalidate previously successful actions. We systematically characterize these variations into six representative categories and observe that such changes do not necessarily invalidate entire procedures: individual transitions can remain reusable when validated against the current task context and interface state. Based on this insight, we propose graph-text templates for selective execution-trace reuse. The graph captures UI states and action transitions, while the text encodes task intent, procedural structure, and typed slots for variable content. A record-template-replay framework constructs templates from verified executions and leverages the current instruction and live UI state to reuse, adapt, or discard individual transitions. Given an execution trace, our framework reduces LLM inference token consumption by approximately 80% on average across five base agents on AndroidWorld, with most agents achieving at least 1.5-fold execution speedup over LLM-only execution. In real-device evaluations on Android and HarmonyOS, our framework achieves action reuse ratios of 70.7-79.8% while maintaining over 2-fold execution speedup in most evaluated configurations.

item.title: End-to-End Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning for Physics-Informed Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimizing high-dimensional physical systems under expensive evaluations and complex constraints is a central challenge in science and engineering. In offline model-based optimization (MBO), methods must improve designs using only a fixed dataset and no test-time access to the true objective. However, existing methods typically suffer from conservatism, unconstrained surrogate exploitation, or function as static inference-time samplers that cannot refine candidates against precise physical objectives. In this paper, we propose Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning (D2C) for offline MBO, which leverages the fact that deterministic sampling makes the reverse denoising chain differentiable with respect to the conditioning signal. D2C turns a frozen conditional diffusion model into an end-to-end gradient-based optimizer by directly optimizing conditioning variables at test time via gradients from frozen surrogate objectives and physics-informed penalties backpropagated through the reverse chain. We implement this idea in a composed proposer-evaluator framework and evaluate it on laser pulse optimization for inertial confinement fusion, sustainable data-center workload scheduling, and four Design-Bench tasks. Our method achieves the strongest results on the two real-world tasks and the best average rank across four Design-Bench tasks.

item.title: Autoregressive Multimodal Anomaly Detection with Large Language Models for Microservice Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microservice systems have become a dominant architecture for large-scale cloud applications, enabling rapid deployment and elastic scaling. However, ensuring the reliability and availability of microservice systems critically relies on effective anomaly detection, as failures and performance anomalies can quickly propagate across services and severely impact end-to-end system behavior. Existing multimodal anomaly detection approaches for microservice systems often struggle with two fundamental limitations: (i) the neglect of modality-specific characteristics in favor of cross-modality fusion, and (ii) the "identity-shortcut" problem that affects the feature reconstruction process. To address these issues, we propose LLMMAD, an autoregressive multimodal anomaly detection framework for microservice systems based on Large Language Models (LLMs). Initially, to reconcile cross-modality fusion with modality-specific preservation, LLMMAD embeds and recombines multimodal data into a unified sequence for LLM processing to model inter-modality relationships, while employing modality-wise reconstruction heads to retain modality-specific information. Subsequently, to eliminate the identity-shortcut, we implement a prediction-driven autoregressive objective, under which the model predicts future states rather than copies current inputs. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that LLMMAD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving F1-score improvements of 3.1%, 1.4%, and 0.9%, respectively, thereby providing a more reliable solution for microservice monitoring.

item.title: Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring aims to detect potentially harmful behaviors in large language models (LLMs) from their CoTs. Intervention-based evaluations measure this property by asking whether a monitor can detect the role of an intervention from the CoT when the targeted behavior occurs, typically using minimal-criterion sensitivity ($\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$) proposed by~\citep{guan2025monitoring}. However, a target behavior observed under intervention is not necessarily caused by it, and we show that this metric can overestimate how often a monitor detects target behaviors actually caused by the intervention. Specifically, we establish $\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$ as an upper bound on this causal detection rate and derive a complementary lower bound, which provides a tighter evaluation framework for CoT monitorability. With this framework, we study whether LLMs can be trained to make their CoTs easier to monitor. We first construct a training dataset of paired control--intervention tasks spanning multiple intervention types. Using the dataset, we design and apply three intervention-specific training methods based on off-policy self-distillation, reinforcement learning, and on-policy self-distillation to train separate variants of each base model. Across various model-monitor configurations, all three methods generally improve CoT monitorability over the corresponding base models under our extended evaluation framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/xinyue-lxy/learning-to-be-monitored.

item.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.

item.title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How well a poetry archive can be searched depends on what the user still remembers, not only on what the model understands. We show this for Classical Arabic poetry, benchmarking nine dense encoders and BM25 over two corpora, three indexing modes and two evaluation protocols. Which retriever wins is governed by how much of a poem's wording the query still carries. On tip-of-the-tongue queries BM25 leads every dense encoder, including an 8B state-of-the-art model (0.746 vs. 0.717 Recall@5); on abstract queries it falls to eighth out of ten (0.392 vs. 0.748). Editing the wording of the same queries shows that this ranking largely reflects query composition: adding one remembered half-verse raises BM25 by 38 points, rewriting the quoted words by hand leaves BM25 level with the 8B encoder, and BM25's sensitivity to remembered wording is significantly steeper than that of the strongest dense encoder. The same axis controls explanation augmentation, whose effect swings from +37 to -39 points.
